characters.name: Obadiah

verses.note: 'The vision of Obadiah. Thus saith the Lord God against Edom, We haue heard a rumour from the Lord, and an ambassadour is sent among the heathen: arise, and let vs rise vp against her to battel.' Obadiah's only self-introduction - no father, hometown, or era is given, just as in KJV. Note the real Geneva word choice: 'against Edom' where KJV reads 'concerning Edom' - a genuine translation-level difference, not a content difference.

funFacts: This Geneva-translation Obadiah is the shortest book in this Bible - one chapter, 21 verses, matching KJV's chapter/verse count exactly.
The 1560 Geneva spelling renders Jacob as 'Iaakob,' Jerusalem as 'Ierusalem,' and Joseph as 'Ioseph' throughout - period orthography (I/J interchange), not a name variant.

characters.name: Edom's Pride and Doom
characters.purpose: Warns that Edom's pride in its rock-fortress dwellings, its famed wisdom, its allied confederates, and its mighty men of Teman will not save it from the Lord's total destruction - even thieves and grape-gatherers leave something behind, but Edom's 'hidden things' will be 'sought vp' completely, and its own confederates will 'driue thee to ye borders' and deceive it.

verses.note: 'The pride of thine heart hath deceiued thee: thou that dwellest in the cleftes of the rockes... that saith in his heart, Who shall bring me downe to the ground?' - Edom's rock-dwelling pride, source of this tier's name.
'Though thou exalt thy selfe as the eagle, and make thy nest among the starres, thence will I bring thee downe, sayth the Lord.'
Thieves and grape-gatherers leave something behind, but Edom ('the things of Esau') will be 'searched' and stripped utterly.
'All the men of thy confederacie haue driuen thee to ye borders... they that eate thy bread, haue laid a wound vnder thee: there is none vnderstanding in him.'
The Lord will 'destroy the wise men out of Edom' and the mount of Esau; Teman's strong men will be 'afraide' and cut off by slaughter.

funFacts: Verse 9 names Teman specifically as a source of dread - an Edomite clan/region proverbially tied to wisdom in the ancient Near East.

characters.name: Violence Against Jacob
characters.purpose: Catalogs Edom's specific cruelty toward its brother nation on the day Jerusalem fell - standing by as strangers cast lots on the city, rejoicing over Judah's ruin, plundering its substance, blocking the crossways to cut off escapees, and shutting up the remnant - teaching that betraying a brother's disaster brings shame and being 'cut off for euer.'

verses.note: 'For thy crueltie against thy brother Iaakob, shame shall couer thee, and thou shalt be cut off for euer.' The Geneva text reads 'crueltie' where KJV reads 'violence' - a real word-choice difference worth noting, same meaning.
'When thou stoodest on the other side... straungers entred into his gates, and cast lots vpon Ierusalem, euen thou wast as one of them.'

A chain of 'shouldest not haue' rebukes: rejoicing over Judah's affliction, speaking proudly in their day of ruin, entering the gate of God's people, laying hands on their substance, standing in the crosse wayes to cut off those escaping, and shutting vp the remnant.

funFacts: Verses 12-14 form the same eight-fold 'shouldest not haue' chain found in KJV, preserved intact in this translation's structure even though individual words (e.g. 'crueltie' vs 'violence') differ.

characters.name: The Day of the Lord
characters.purpose: Promises the day of the Lord is near vpon all the heathen and that Edom's own deeds will 'returne vpon thine head'; deliuerance and holiness rest on mount Zion, the house of Iaakob and house of Ioseph become fire and flame against the house of Esau's stubble, scattered Israel repossesses its territory, and the book closes with 'the kingdome shalbe the Lords.'

verses.note: 'For the day of the Lord is neere, vpon all the heathen: as thou hast done, it shall bee done to thee: thy reward shall returne vpon thine head.'

'But vpon mount Zion shalbe deliuerance... the house of Iaakob shalbe a fire, and the house of Ioseph a flame, and the house of Esau as stubble... there shall bee no remnant of the house of Esau for the Lord hath spoken it.'
Restored possession of the mount of Esau, the plaine of the Philistims, the fieldes of Ephraim and Samaria, Gilead for Beniamin, and captiuitie possessing land vnto Zarephath and Sepharad.

'And they that shall saue, shall come vp to mount Zion to iudge the mount of Esau, and the kingdome shalbe the Lords.' Geneva's 'they that shall saue' (plural agents) reads slightly differently from KJV's 'saviours shall come up' but conveys the same closing declaration of divine kingship.

funFacts: Verse 20's 'Sepharad' is unique to this verse in scripture; later Jewish tradition (not the text itself) connected it to Spain, the origin of the term 'Sephardic.'

characters.name: Jacob (Iaakob)

verses.note: 'For thy crueltie against thy brother Iaakob' - Edom's guilt grounded in the Esau/Jacob kinship from Genesis; a personification of the nation, not an individually-acting figure within this book.
'The house of Iaakob' paired with 'the house of Ioseph' is promised deliuerance on mount Zion and becomes fire against the house of Esau.

funFacts: Spelled 'Iaakob' throughout this 1560 Geneva text (period I/J spelling), the same figure as Jacob in the Genesis index - flagged as a spelling variant, not a separate character.
Verse 18's 'house of Ioseph' is this book's only mention of Joseph, named only as a co-agent of judgment, with no individual action of his own.

characters.name: Esau

verses.note: 'Howe are the things of Esau sought vp, and his treasures searched?' - Edom's plundering, addressed via its ancestor's name.
Wise men 'out of Edom' and understanding 'from the mount of Esau' destroyed; every one 'of the mount of Esau shalbe cut off by slaughter.'
'The house of Esau as stubble' - consumed by the fire and flame of Jacob and Joseph until there is 'no remnant of the house of Esau.'
'The mount of Esau' is repeatedly named as territory and people judged and possessed by Israel's restored remnant.

funFacts: Every reference to Esau in this book names the nation (Edom) or its territory ('mount of Esau'), never an individual action - consistent with the KJV's treatment of the same book.

spellingVariantsNote.note: This 1560 Geneva text spells Jacob as 'Iaakob' and Joseph as 'Ioseph' (period I/J typographical convention) and Jerusalem as 'Ierusalem' - these are the same figures as their standard-spelled counterparts elsewhere in the Character Index, not distinct characters, flagged here per the naming-collision discipline even though no real collision exists, only an orthographic one.

otherObadiahsInScripture.note: Same naming-collision caution as the KJV Obadiah index applies here: 'Obadiah' ('servant of the Lord') is a very common Old Testament name (e.g. the governor of Ahab's house in 1 Kings 18, several genealogical listings in Chronicles/Ezra/Nehemiah). This 1560 Geneva text's Obadiah 1:1 gives no genealogical or biographical detail linking this prophet to any of them - not indexed individually here since this file covers Obadiah only; see the KJV Obadiah.json for the full corrected list of scriptural namesakes.

notes: Read directly from E:/Unity/Clicker_Genesis/Assets/Resources/Verses/Geneva/obadiah_31.json (the real 1560 Geneva extraction) before drafting. This Geneva-translation Obadiah is structurally and content-identical to the KJV Obadiah already indexed in this project - same 1 chapter, same 21 verses, same four-movement shape (prophet's introduction, Edom's pride and predicted doom vv.1-9, Edom's specific cruelty against brother Jacob during Jerusalem's fall vv.10-14, the Day of the LORD and Zion's restoration vv.15-21). No real canonical/structural differences were found versus KJV for this book - unlike some other Geneva/Ethiopian books in this project (e.g. the Ethiopian Bible's 9-chapter Ezra), this is the same text, differing only in period 1560 English spelling/word choice: 'Iaakob' for Jacob, 'Ierusalem' for Jerusalem, 'Ioseph' for Joseph, 'Beniamin' for Benjamin, 'Philistims' for Philistines, and a handful of real translation-level word choices worth flagging without altering meaning or structure - verse 1 reads 'against Edom' where KJV reads 'concerning Edom,' and verse 10 reads 'crueltie' where KJV reads 'violence.' Scribe tiers and manager/law-tier ids are suffixed '_geneva' throughout to avoid any collision with the existing KJV Obadiah.json ids (obadiah, edom_pride_and_doom, violence_against_jacob, day_of_the_lord, jacob, esau), per the project's cross-translation id-collision-avoidance rule. Jacob and Esau again appear only as personifications of Israel and Edom respectively, never as individually-acting characters within this book itself, matching the KJV draft's treatment - included as 'named' cross-reference entries rather than managers. No scripture text was altered, paraphrased, or reinterpreted; all verse notes quote or closely paraphrase the actual extracted Geneva wording.
